newsitem.title: USA: Thomson unveils RCA Network Computer, WebTV rival.
newsitem.headline: Thomson unveils RCA Network Computer, WebTV rival.

text.p: Thomson Consumer Electronics, a developer of the Digital Satellite System, Thursday introduced a set-top box device that turns a television into a low-cost Internet access device via a telephone line.

The RCA Network Computer, one of the first major competitors of a similar product by WebTV Networks Inc., will be available nationwide in September, at $349 with a wireless keyboard and $299 for a base model with a wired keyboard.
The device is the first consumer product based on standards developed by Oracle Corp. and its Network Computer unit.

"Web TV is a box that allows you to surf the Web on your TV and this integrates computer technology into the TV," said Bonnie Crater, vice president of strategic marketing at Network Computer. "WebTV is a great first-generation product; this is a great second-generation product."
Also, unlike the WebTV, the RCA Network Computer can be hooked up to a standard personal computer printer. WebTV is addressing this criticism in a new software upgrade.
WebTV, which is also priced in the $300 range, is sold by partners Sony Corp. and Philips Electronics NV. About 85,000 units have been sold since its launch last year.
Other firms coming out with TV devices based on Oracle specifications include Zenith Electronics Corp.

"We are the first ones to take network computing into the home," said Louis Lenzi, vice president of multimedia products and services at Thomson, the U.S. operations for Thomson Multimedia, which is a unit of Paris-based Thomson SA.
Lenzi said the RCA Network Computer provides a more personalized delivery of information to consumers than WebTV, which signed a deal to be acquired by Microsoft Corp.
The deal, announced in April and valued at $425 million, is still pending and has yet to receive regulatory approval.
Lenzi said RCA is targeting the 60 million U.S. homes with TV sets but no personal computers, and 20 million homes with PCs but no modems for online and Internet access.
But Thomson and Oracle executives would not give any projections on how many RCA units will sell.

NetChannel Inc., a privately held company in South San Francisco, Calif., will provide Internet access for an additional $19.95 a month. NetChannel said its service is personalized with specialised entertainment content for RCA users, an electronic programme guide and electronic mail.
Thomson said it plans a national retail rollout in September but it does not yet plan a hefty television campaign, in the way that it rolled out the Digital Satellite System (DSS) in 1994.

DSS was one of the most successful consumer electronics rollouts, and Thomson initially had heavy in-store promoting and advertising with its retailers and later did a national TV advertising campaign.

"I think the NetChannel service is a lot closer to what we are going to need to get people really interested in this," said Josh Bernoff, a Forrester Research analyst. "It's a lot more TV-like. ... There is a fundamental problem here; until the Web is a lot more entertaining and until it's better integrated with TV, (Internet access and TV) is an odd mix."
"You are not going to see this category take off just because RCA has a product," Bernoff said, adding that Sony and Magnavox, the Philips brand, are not exactly off-brands in TV.
Forrester expects the "Internet-enabled TV" market to grow to about 100,000 households this year, 400,000 in 1998 and 3.2 million in the year 2000.
